Day 3, morning. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] crossed the garden past the wooden treehouse observatory and found Marcos among the olive trees. He asked him directly: what is really on the other side of the hill, and why doesn't anyone talk about it. Marcos tapped his walking stick twice — his sign that a true answer is coming — and answered in his own circling way, with a story about why the shepherds always come down from the pines by dusk. He would not say what is over the hill. He said only that the hill teaches differently to each person who climbs it, that he does not know what it will show [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], and that this not-telling is itself the answer: some things have to be found, not given.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood that Marcos had said everything he was going to say, and that the rest was his to go and discover. The chapter ends with him standing in the garden, near the wooden treehouse observatory, his hands empty, the day stretching out ahead of him, the hill still waiting.

Who knows what: Marcos still has not said what he knows about the other side, only that the hill will teach it. Rosa (from Day 2) knows [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] is climbing the hill; the village has not said what is beyond it.

Still open: what is over the hill; what Marcos actually knows and is withholding; what [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] is really afraid of.
